The Session

Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

Added by Roger Gall on February 1st, 2012

Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

The Live Music Bill will become law soon so it is clear then.

Sessions are either
1 Not PERFORMANCES of live music and therefore not Regulated Entertainment and which are free from any requirement for ADDITIONAL entertainment licensing at any time and from any condition imposed on any other form of Regulated Entertainment taking place at the venue.

2. PERFORMANCES of live music which are Regulated Entertainment but which are exempt from any requirement for ADDITIONAL entertainment licensing in qualfying small venues under the Live Music Bill, from 8am to 11pm but which automatically become subject to the requirement as Regulated Entertainment at 11pm to 8am and will for this period, also become subject to any other conditions imposed on any other form of Regulated Entertainment taking place in the venue.

3. PERFORMANCES of live music which are Regulated Entertainment but which are exempt from any requirement for ADDITIONAL entertainment licensing at any time as a PERFORMANCE of live music which is incidental etc and exempt from any condition imposed on any other form of Regulated Entertainment taking place at the venue.

As you can see the legality of sessions in venues which do not have Additional Entertainment Licensing Permission depends on what your local licensing authority (the council) understands to be PERFORMANCE.

Is there anyone in England & Wales who have a council with policy which does not consider sessions to be a licensable PERFORMANCE of live music and therefore legal without the venue having to apply for additional entertainment licensing permission?

Is there anyone who considers that sessions are PERFORMANCE and are NOT threatened by having to find a licensee that is prepared to pay and go through the required red tape to enable them as conventional paid entertainment?

Is there anyone who considers that sessions are not PERFORMANCE and are threatened by having to find a licensee that is prepared to pay and go through the required red tape to enable them as conventional paid entertainment?

Part 1
General definitions
The provision of regulated entertainment…..

1)The descriptions of entertainment are—
(a)a performance of a play,.
(b)an exhibition of a film,.
(c)an indoor sporting event,.
(d)a boxing or wrestling entertainment,.
(e)a performance of live music,.
(f)any playing of recorded music,.
(g)a performance of dance,.
*****(h)entertainment of a similar description to that falling within paragraph (e), (f) or (g),.
where the entertainment takes place in the presence of an audience and is provided for the purpose, or for purposes which include the purpose, of entertaining that audience.*****

Licensing Act 2003

The Live Music Bill defines “Live Music” thus:

"“live music” means entertainment of a description falling within,
or of a similar description to that falling within, paragraph
2(1)(e) of Schedule 1;"

It’s that “similar description” bit that puts your argument in the waste bin.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

>What societal evil is this law intended to suppress? Or is it just a way to collect more licensing fees?<

The four objectives of the Act are:
the prevention of crime and disorder,
public safety,
prevention of public nuisance, and
the protection of children from harm

Prior to the Licensing Act 2003, local authorities set their own fee levels for additional entertainment licensing permission - the Act removed this and the level is now set by central Govt. It would be fair to say that there is a lobby by local authorities for a return to this.

The LGA Group lobby were originally against the Live Music Bill but although being supportive of the Govt’s own proposals to ease the entertainment licensing burden for non musical activites - they are now strongly against any further easing of the additional entertainment licensing burden for live music, as the following will show.

http://www.local.gov.uk/web/10161/legislation/-/journal_content/56/10161/3168126/ARTICLE-TEMPLATE

The premise on which the strong lobby for the continuation of additional entertainment licensing for live music is based, is that, in advance of a note of music being sounded, live music and musicians will automatically present concerns which existing planning, environmental, health, safety and other legislation is inadequate to deal with and which only additional entertainment licensing permission is adequate to deal with.

I suggest we have all been to sessions like this………….

“ don’t think that a session where players are facing one another round a table can be regarded as regulated entertainment. It is not a performance directed at an audience. It says that to be ”regulated entertainment“ the entertainment must take place in the presence of an audience and be provided for the purpose of, or for purposes which include, entertaining that audience. If the session takes place completely disregarding the audience it can’t be regulated entertainment”

I think you’ve missed the point.

The Live Music Bill makes the session “Live Music” and the only criteria after that is that it has to be “in the presence of an audience”. An audience is one or more person/s who are able to hear the music - that includes the members of the public who are actually playing the music. If you don’t regard yourself as members of the public, then it would suggest that you are employed by the licensee (not necessarily paid a monetary fee). If you are employed by the licensee, you are performing a service. Then it is a performance. Either way, it is live music in the presence of an audience, and similar enough (as outlined in Part 1, (2), (h) - “similar description”) to Part 1, (2), (e), to be regarded as live music that requires regulation under the Act as amended by the Bill.
If there was nobody else other than the musicians at your session, that doesn’t say too much about your session, but you are still members of the public, and the intention of the licensee is surely to entertain the public, be it those playing in the session (who, hopefully, are actually listening to each other) or those merely listening.

It’s not that complicated, and the Act makes it fairly plain, as far as Acts go.

“Music tuition will not require a licence as the music (and the premises) is not being provided for the entertainment of an audience, but for the purpose of educating those present”

That’s why they call a school a school and a public bar a pub.

“Educating” my erse.

“Do does anyone here really think that sessions should be thought of as a crimnal activity and be happy to leave it so? ”

Dear me, you haven’t just missed the point, you are creating your own.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“Note that the words of the legislation do not contain any reference to there being a secondary offence nor to aiding, abetting, counselling nor to a primary offence.”

Irrelevant. What it does say expressly, is that the musician would not be committing an offence by playing the music.
Ergo- the people actually making the music are not committing an offence. The primary offence is the one that the Act establishes. In this case, it relates to licensing of premises, and the person responsible for obtaining a licence and subsequently holding that licence is known as a licensee. Therefore, only the licensee (or proprietor) is capable of committing the primary offence of allowing the premises to be used for regulated entertainment without authorisation (a licence).
Nobody else could be prosecuted for not having a licence, as they are not responsible for obtaining a licence. Not having a licence is the primary offence. Any offence by a person not responsible for obtaining a licence would be secondary to that primary offence (an accessory). The Act doesn’t have to expressly state this. It’s the kind of thing anyone with half a brain might be expected to work out for themselves.

“Let’s see if I have this right?”

No. You have it wrong.

All the various instances whereby assisting or encouraging someone to commit an offence do not have to be worded in an Act of Parliament that sets out the conditions in which an offence is committed. It is enough to be aware that assisting in any crime could be seen as aiding, abetting, counselling or procuring the commission of that crime. Likewise inchoate offences, like plotting, conspiring or inciting the commission of a crime.
The, criminal offence of conspiracy, for example, comes under a separate Act, The Criminal Law Act, 1977. This makes it an offence “if a person agrees with any other person or persons that a course of conduct shall be pursued which will necessarily amount to or involve the commission of any offence or offences by one or more of the parties to the agreement if the agreement is carried out in accordance with their intentions”.
The offence of conspiracy does not need to be included in any Act relating to a criminal offence for conspiring to commit that crime to be an offence in itself. That the actual crime that the offender was conspiring to commit is established in law is enough.

However, the actual circumstances that could be considered a primary offence under a particular Act would be expected to be worded in the Act.

It’s not that difficult, surely?

“Perhaps we can leave this particular issue for folk to judge?”

I doubt if you are capable of judging anything with any level of competence.

Mainly because noise pollution is already being regulated differently at this time of night, when special requirements kick-in.

The current requirement for existing entertainment licensing is already additional to the existing planning, environmental health & safety and other legislation. The argument proposed for the 11pm curfew - when performances of live music must obtain additional entertainment licensing (or more correctly for retaining this requirement from 11pm until 8am) is bizzare - for it the very opposite argument.

The 11pm time (when additional entertainment licensing permission is automatically required) is thought to be a good idea precisely because the different anti-noise pollution legislation referred to earlier also - kicks-in at 11pm.

This is more than a little strange when you think about it - as additional entertainment licensing permission is of little help in dealing with actual and measurable noise pollution.

You cannot ask for permission to make noise pollution and the local authority cannot grant it . Any noise pollution from any source will have to be dealt the same whether additional entertaiment licensing permission is in place or not.

However, additional entertainment licensing permission is a very good way of preventing and limiting live music (often in advance of a note being sounded) - even non-amplfied sessions which are very unlikely to cause any measurable noise pollution.

It may not bother you that providing an activity that you value (after 11pm) without additional entertainment licensing permission, will still remain a criminal offence - even after the Live Music Bill has managed to clear away some of the offending legislation. Or that the pub that you were playing in will be able to serve alcohol long after the music has to stop.

It was over 10 years ago since a supportive licensee and friend received a letter which demanded that they either stop the session or pay for the then PEL - and that they could face prosecution and a possible maximum £20,000 fine or 6 months in prison if we continued.

In that time there has been a failure to educate the general public and local authorities about what sessions are (or are not) their true value and role.

And in particular of the threat presented to them by the requirement for a third party (the licensee of the few remaining ans suitable venues) to be prepared to obtain additional entertainment permission to enable sessions to legally tale place as Regulated Entertainment.

In that time - the Morris dancing lobby has managed to obtain exemptions which now mean that their activity is totally free from this requirement, even when the music is amplified.

Perhaps that lobby get the treatment they deserve?

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

One of the key differences in this legislation is that it is essentially European in character.

As anyone with experience of Europe will know, the crucial difference over there is that there is a general presumption that any given thing is illegal unless it can be shown to be otherwise. If not, then this is presumably because the law is not yet sufficiently precise and only requires to be suitably extended.

British law ( and here I use the term as a catch-all for the somewhat different English and Scottish systems ) are based on the assumption that any given thing is legal unless it can be shown otherwise. More to the point, there is a large body of case law and precedent demonstrating that where some given action is arguably illegal but no identifiable harm results, that action is for practical purposes legal in effect and need not be a matter for action.

It is easy to satirise this ( Terry Pratchett’s running gag about “the long-drawn out chord required by law to indicate that folk music is about to be perpetrated”, for example ) but it is an important principle. Not so many years ago, a landlord could conduct his business on the basis that there were a limited range of activities which were clearly illegal, and others which were not. Now, it seems he must conduct his business on the basis that almost anything may be ruled illegal, on pain of forfeiture of his livelihood.

Not a good situation

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“If allowing your premises to be used for such activity is illegal, then the activity itself is in effect illegal, since it cannot take place without some premises in which to be held. ”

Rubbish. You fail to understand a basic principle.

If the activity itself were deemed to be illegal, then the actus reus would be the activity itself. The performer of the activity ( the musician) would be held accountable. This is licensing law, whereby the owner, or proprietor of the premises is expected to obtain a licence for provision of entertainment. Failing to obtain this licence, and providing that entertainment without a licence (allowing the entertainment to take place) in spite of there being no authorisation is the actus reus. The provider/licensee is held accountable.
It clearly states in the Act that where the licensable activity is provision of regulated entertainment, if someone’s only involvement in the provision of entertainment is the actual performance of that entertainment, then there is no offence committed on their part- in other words, no actus reus - the actual performance of the music is not an offence. It is the provision of that entertainment, the allowing of it to take place, and the organisation, without the necessary authorisation.

All the nonsense about Soviet legal process, immigrants controlling things etc.

Perhaps, when it’s realised that licensing of entertainment started with that Act which came into force in 1752, it will be understood that there has been a major improvement in this latest Bill.

That was the Preamble to the Disorderly Houses Act of 1751. Which, incidentally, was finally repealed in full in 2008 (only Section 8 was in force, which deemed that the person in charge of a “disorderly house” was also the keeper, and liable). It was in the reign of George II, and it was believed that places of public entertainment were a major cause of theft and robbery because those who frequented such places blew all their dosh and had to resort to crime in order to survive. The Act regulated places of entertainment by requiring that a licence be obtained from the magistrates (it is still a common law offence to keep a “disorderly house” despite the repeal of the Act). There was no specification of what constituted performance, or the stipulation that it be before an audience etc. Just “public dancing, music or other public entertainment” (which still is the basis of entertainment legislation, though things are more specific). Through time, various parts of the Act were repealed, as those aspects became drafted into separate legislation, and in the sixties, the responsibility of licensing and enforcement moved to the local authority. I would be surprised if the local authorities welcomed this.
All the various Acts which regulated entertainment prior to the Licensing Act 2003 were not really that much different. It is the Live Music Act which makes a giant leap forward in the way live music is treated by the authorities.

And here we have someone who seems to think it’s all still doom and gloom. Along with some character who thinks he knows whats going on because he travels all over the place (yet he doesn’t even understand “volenti non fit injuria” -it’s not about “no harm done” it’s about voluntarily placing yourself at risk) and sees everything as a result of this right wing vision of European intervention (he’s been there - not grasping the fact that other European states have their respective domestic law, and we are subject to EC regulations just as they are) and immigration are behind perceived evils.

No, it’s not about Soviet legislation. It’s down to antiquated Georgian legislation, and the couple of centuries and more that it has taken to at least remove the requirement of a licence between certain hours for live music.

Yeah - I have been ranting here for a good bit. Anyway, Dr Dow, you won’t need your bog roll for a while.

The following is from the S 182 Guidance to the Licensing Act 2003.

>SPONTANEOUS MUSIC, SINGING
AND DANCING
3.24 The spontaneous performance of music, singing or dancing does not amount to the provision of regulated entertainment and is not a licensable activity.

The relevant part of the 2003 Act to consider in this context is paragraph 1(3) of Schedule 1 to the Act. This states that the second condition which must apply before an activity constitutes the provision of regulated entertainment is that the premises (meaning “any place”) at which the entertainment is, or entertainment facilities are, provided are made available for the purpose, or purposes which include the purpose, of enabling the entertainment concerned to take place.

In the case of genuinely spontaneous music (including singing) and dancing, the place where the entertainment takes place will not have been made available to those taking part for that purpose.<

There is only one licence now. A premises licence. Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“That was in the discussion on and made there, in reference only to the situation in Scotland. There it had always been considered that the licence required permission to serve alcohol was generally enough to cover entertainment.”

Considering that there were seven types of licence prior to the current licensing legislation (in force since 2009) and The Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982 actually clarified the requirement or not for entertainment licensing (still requiring licensing for late night [outwith permitted hours] entertainment - and, if the entertainment is “significant”, it changes the classification of the premises), I’d say that you are making a stab in the dark.

The current legislation [The Licensing (Scotland) Act 2005/The Premises Licence (Scotland) Regulations 2007] put an end to the seven types of licence. They also require, like in the England and Wales Act, an initial description of all activities that will take place (in this case, called an “Operating Plan”) on the premises (and what measures are in place to protect the “objectives” - the same “objectives” of the E&W Act). Any variation to the initial activities would require an application for variation.

“A situation that many of us would have liked to have been adopted in England and Wales. ”

You’ve got it. It’s just that the definition of entertainment is more specific than “significant”. As long as the “entertainment” is as described (not just ticking a box - there are issues such as sound proofing relative to the kind of entertainment, etc - the type of entertainment has to be specified) in the original “operating schedule”, the licence to sell alcohol on the premises also covers any entertainment. If not, you have to apply for a variation.

The Live Music Act will create a class of entertainment considered not “significant” enough to warrant a licensable activity, requiring accommodation in the premises licence. It’s just that the “significance” is defined in the Act, and is somewhat narrower than in the Scottish equivalent that differentiates it,.

If you don’t understand any of that, it means that you don’t really understand the relevant licensing laws. If you don’t understand the licensing laws, you really shouldn’t be waffling on about them.

Thats interesting, with reference to scotland there’s always been a facility for bars to extend licensing hours on Fridays Thursdays and Saturday nights, to 01:00 AM and 11:30 PM on Saturday.

This extension is known as an “entertainments license” and requires the publican/license holder to host live entertainment to qualify for the extension.

Back in the day before there was a regular Thursday night session locally, I remember one publican, who’d tried and failed to book the duet I played in, comment at our suggestion he host a regular Thursday night session that, the local licensing board didn’t consider a session to be entertainment and that it was considered normal pub craic. He reckoned his license would be on a shoogly peg if he were to stay open late with only a session as a pretext, given the attitudes of the issuing board.

Times have changed and sessions are considered adequate as qualifying entertainment these days. Interestingly, it’s not the fact that there’s a session happening that requires any form of approval/license, it’s the extension to normal hours that requires the license extension.

↳ Posted by Solidmahog on February 12th, 2012.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

"Thats interesting, with reference to scotland there’s always been a facility for bars to extend licensing hours on Fridays Thursdays and Saturday nights, to 01:00 AM and 11:30 PM on Saturday.

This extension is known as an “entertainments license” and requires the publican/license holder to host live entertainment to qualify for the extension. "

It hasn’t always been there, Solidmahog. It came with the Licensing (Scotland) Act 1976 (Section 64). It is called an “entertainments licence”, but, in actuality it was the granting of an extension if “having regard to the social circumstances of the locality in which the premises in respect of which the application is made are situated or to activities taking place in that locality, the board considers it is desirable to do so”.

That Act also set the permitted hours (I mentioned that earlier, though not with the same clarity as you). Subsequent legislation altered things. One piece of legislation stipulated:

[47
(1)A licensing board shall not grant an application under section 64 of the principal Act for an extension of permitted hours unless it is satisfied by the applicant, taking account of the factors mentioned in subsection (3) of that section— .
(a)that there is a need in the locality in which the premises in respect of which the application is made are situated for a regular extension of the permitted hours; and .
(b)that such an extension is likely to be of such benefit to the community as a whole as to outweigh any detriment to that locality.]

Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) (Scotland) Act 1990

So, your publican might have been on the right track!

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“There is no need to apply a set time of night (11pm) when additional entertainment licensing permission will be automatically required, on grounds of potential noise”

You obviously don’t know how licensing works.

The Noise Act is concerned with noise that is considered excessive, and any “legal powers” given under the Clean Neighbourhoods and Environment Act 2005, in relation to the Noise Act relate to powers after the “noise” has been made.

The threshold of 11pm (which I don’t agree with) is a move to prevent excessive noise and nuisance, rather than cure it.
If a variation of a licence is applied for, then objections can be made by certain bodies (including residents) and a hearing would decide whether there was a risk of excessive noise, and if it was felt that there was, the variation would be rejected.

Also, the risk would be assessed on the existing levels in the area (cumulative), so if there are already a few places with late night entertainment, it would be taken into consideration. It’s not just the noise, it’s the general “nuisance” aspect.

It’s not “automatic”. It depends on several factors, and objections.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“But the conventional paid performer in a pub situation, whether an actual contract exists or not - could well be said to be one who was in in the temporary employ of the licensee.”

The word “employ” is loaded. It has several interpretations. Certainly there would be a more legally binding contract - consideration of monetary value.

“A pub’s customers are not. ‘Simples’ ”

As said before - you can’t have it both ways. If the musicians are “pub customers” they are the “public” - which is your audience. If you had to ask permission to play, and it was granted, that is a contract - in its most basic form. It might not be legally binding, nor conform to more exacting legal definitions, but it is a contract. The agreement was that you could use the premises to play music. Playing the music means that the licensee has fulfilled his part - the premises have been used - and your part has been fulfilled - the music has been played. You have performed the contract by way of playing music. The music is the performance on your part.

Whatever the situation with the PRS, the relevant legislation quite clearly, and unambiguously defines performance in relation to copyright. That it is set in statute would mean that it carries weight as to a particular definition of the word.
Both these arguments would put you on thin ice if you were to challenge the law on the definition of the word.

“So the Govt obviously don’t know how licensing works either?”

The government, I’m sure, are pretty clued up on how licensing works. However, you’ve cherry picked the paragraph:

[This consultation does not propose applying an 11pm cut off for the deregulation of regulated entertainment. This is because existing legal powers in the Noise Act 1996 already make special provision to deal with problems occurring after 11pm for alcohol licensed premises, which will cover the vast majority of venues for entertainment. Noise Act powers work in tandem with the Licensing Act 2003 so that any premises that is not abiding by its licence conditions can be immediately tackled by Local Authority officers, but it should be noted that most Local Authorities do not operate a full nuisance complaints service outside normal working hours.]

See that bit at the end? In order to “tackle” any noise problems, there would have to be a complaint raised, and someone to receive the complaint, in order to exercise the “Noise Act Powers”. Far simpler, in the first instance, to limit the possibility of noise problems by licensing the possible source of any noise problems (either the music or the crowd) after a cut off period. I think Dave has been trying to tell you this several times. It’s about working “in tandem” rather than relying on curing the problem once it occurs - which would be a solo operated cycle. That the licensing process involves consultation from “interested parties” and provides a vehicle to set conditions on a license, means that the “prevention is better than cure” principle is given weight.
Baroness Rawlings placed a caveat on support of the Bill, mentioning that Labour’s earlier consultation was predicated on an 11 pm cut-off point, and also pointed out how the licensing process has certain integral “protections”. That was her ground for changing the cut-off from midnight to 11 pm.

I don’t think it was a strong enough ground, but I can see the reasoning. It was about the extra “safeguard” of the licensing “protection” over the practicality of tackling the envisaged problem after it had already taken place.

I really don’t see why you are still so concerned about this hour’s difference. I mean, even Morris dancers are thin on the ground after 11 pm. Yep, I would have preferred the cut-off to have been midnight, but it’s better than nowt.

“ It is an element of the situation that comprises a ”staged event“ rather than a spontaneous performance.”

Not at all. A spontaneous performance is just that. Something that is unplanned. The presence or not of an audience is immaterial. It could be a silent mime act, completely unplanned. It would still be a spontaneous performance. If it was billed as a performance, it would be a planned (or staged) event, and still wouldn’t rely on the presence of an audience to become a performance. The audience factor is immaterial. However, if a performance of music reaches the ears of the public, it would be hard to deny that it reached a public audience. If the performers are something other than members of the public, then it is a planned and staged event, provision of which was made by the licensee (the use of the premises) and if the venue is open to the public, then the potential of a public audience is there, and it would be regarded as intended for a public audience. Application would need to be made for variation of a licence (I think 28 days in advance) if the licence doesn’t already cover it, and notice would need to be made available to the public and all interested parties. Basically, it would be licensable if there was intent for the music to reach the ears of the public.

Again, either the musicians are intentionally there to play in public, or they are the public.

13.55 The Secretary of State recommends that statements of policy should provide clear indications of how the licensing authority will secure the proper integration of its licensing policy with local crime prevention, planning, transport, tourism, race equality schemes, and cultural strategies and any other plans introduced for the management of town centres and the night-time economy. Many of these strategies are not directly related to the promotion of the four licensing objectives, but, indirectly, impact upon them. Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

Let’s look at the situation in the not too distant future. It is assumed (with good reason) that sessions qualify as “regulated entertainment” at present.

Under the Live Music Act 2012, sessions will be exempt from licensing requirements if they take place between 8 am and 11 pm on the same day.

If a licensee wishes to extend the session beyond 11 pm, then, so long as the “operating schedule” already allows the sale or supply of alcohol during the period in which it is wished to provide the music, then he/she can apply for a minor variation to the licence [under The Legislative Reform (Minor Variations to Premises Licences and Club Premises Certificates) Order 2009]
. This involves completion of an application form, and costs £89.
The local authority would need to be satisfied that the variation is minor, and will likely contact the relevant “responsible authorities” to determine the impact on the “objectives” of the Act. If the licensee has any savvy, he/she would have worded the application to satisfy the local authority that the objectives were being met.

Anyway - after that, the licensee is required to notify the public of the application by displaying a notice on a white sheet of paper on the premises, for ten days, commencing on the working day after the application was submitted to the local authority.

Unless good ground for objection is given by the “responsible authorities” (and this doesn’t include the licensing authority), then the licensing authority are obliged to grant the minor variation.

So, very shortly, sessions will not require licensing if they don’t go on past 11 pm. If they do, it will cost the licensee £89 to permit it.
Have a whip round if that’s a problem. Otherwise stop whinging

89 quid, Roger. That’s what you are whinging over.

Still struggling?

The guidance is for application, not “turning a blind eye”.

The local authority can only act within the provisions of the Act. It cannot act ultra vires. To be intra vires, then the Act must be adhered to.

The guidance is there:

1.6 The Guidance is provided for licensing
authorities carrying out their functions. It also
provides information for magistrates hearing
appeals against licensing decisions and has
been made widely available for the benefit of
operators of licensed premises, their legal
advisers and the general public. It is a key
mechanism for promoting best practice,
ensuring consistent application of licensing
powers across the country and for promoting
fairness, equal treatment and proportionality.

In other words, any application of the law by the local authority (licensing requirements) must be consistent with the law.
The local authority cannot operate ultra vires (without authority - ie outwith the provisions of the relevant law), therefore it can only operate within the powers given to it. It cannot make the law, only follow the law, and any licensing requirements (conditions imposed on the licence) must be consistent with the guidance. Look here, buddy boy:

1.8 Nothing in this Guidance should be taken as
indicating that any requirement of licensing
law or any other law may be overridden
(including the obligations placed on the
authorities under human rights legislation).
The Guidance does not in any way replace
the statutory provisions of the 2003 Act or add
to its scope and licensing authorities should
note that interpretation of the Act is a matter
for the courts. Licensing authorities and others
using the Guidance must take their own
professional and legal advice about its
implementation.

If the local authority were to be made aware, expressly that an offence was being committed, they cannot “override it”.

That means the letter from the councillor (which would be on record) indicated that music was being provided without a licence. Follow?

Now, what is expected of the licensing authority?

Well, they can impose conditions on a licence, they can require that certain measures are put in place before a licence is granted. Lookie here, buddy:

GENERAL PRINCIPLES

1.14 If an application for a premises licence or club
premises certificate has been made lawfully
and there have been no representations from
responsible authorities or interested parties,
the licensing authority must grant the
application, subject only to conditions that are
consistent with the operating schedule and
relevant mandatory conditions.

Each application on its own merits

1.15 Each application must be considered on its
own merits and any conditions attached to
licences and certificates must be tailored to
the individual style and characteristics of the
premises and events concerned. This is
essential to avoid the imposition of
disproportionate and overly burdensome
conditions on premises where there is no need
for such conditions. Standardised conditions
should be avoided and indeed, may be
unlawful where they cannot be shown to be
necessary for the promotion of the licensing
objectives in any individual case.

Hopefully, by now, you are beginning to see what this guidance malarkey is all about, though I doubt it.

One more paragraph:

Avoiding duplication of other legal
requirements

1.16 The licensing authority should only impose
conditions on a premises licence or club
premises certificate which are necessary and
proportionate for the promotion of the
licensing objectives. If other existing law
already places certain statutory responsibilities
on an employer or operator of premises, it
cannot be necessary to impose the same or
similar duties on the premises licence holder
or club. It is only where additional and
supplementary measures are necessary to
promote the licensing objectives that
necessary, proportionate conditions will need
to be attached to a licence.

This enforcement was based on the (still untested) legal argument) that any pub customer making any form of live music for their own enjoyment, was a performer and that any more than two such performers could not be exempt under the partial exemption known as the .‘two-in-a-bar’ rule.

Some months after this - I managed to get this enforcement reviewed by a council committee. In truth the elected councillors were very sympathetic and did make a number of suggestions and agreed to contact central Govt on some aspects.

However, as the agenda item presented by the employees to the meeting was simply asking for this enforcement, (and the interpretation on which is was based) to be endorsed - there was no question that it would be.

To do otherwise was for the committee to find that its own employees had done something wrong - and that can never be.

So you could argue that this enforcement was agreed council policy but would have to accept that it was not the case when the action (which established the policy) was taken.

Perhaps, and we will never know this - had the meeting taken place before the enforcement - the enforcement may not have taken place?

That is why I am suggesting a process which would kick-in whenever there was any question being raised that the activity was not licensable.

As the Licensing Act requires every Licensing Authority to form a Licensing Committee with a remit for all licensing matters - it would appear that such a process is already in place.

But not used.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

I corrected “audience” to public, Dave.

At the time of the case, provision of equipment was not licensable, but singing along with a recording (or, as this case established, generated music) was.
However, It was also stated in obiter that if more than two people performed in the course of an event, even though there were never more than two performing at one time, then there was no exemption under Section 182 of the Licensing Act, 1964 (the two in a bar rule didn’t apply). This was in relation to karaoke singers, but obviously applied to any situation.

Hence, if two members of the public entertained other members of the public, followed by another two members of that public entertaining that public, then one section of the public entertaining another section of the public is licensable (then it had to be more than two all told). Entertaining the public by the public is a licensable activity - paid or not.

That was the point.

They are obliged to transfer (and I used the word “interpret” in that respect earlier, not in a judicial sense) this into a working policy. I have yet to see a policy that doesn’t do this reasonably.
The inference they have made regarding expressed wording of the Act and the possible implications of the same, seem quite reasonable - very reasonable, in fact.
The only way it could be challenged is in court. The only way it can come to court is by appeal (which requires declaring the activity in the first place) or by ignoring it and subsequent prosecution and appearance in court.
The former seems the most sensible - the licensee should apply for a variation and question the need for variation. Any decision from the licensing panel affecting the licence can be appealed.
Or would you rather the local authority pounded the streets looking for violations and bringing charges, in order for a court to decide?

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“It may be the case that this is the only way that a correctly processed council POLICY could be challenged (without the council itself deciding to change it) but these four so-called requirements for qualification for this exemption - were never even claimed to be the council’s correctly processed council POLICY - were they? ”

That is incoherent.

The fundamental principle behind all this (even way back when licensing of entertainment was first required by law) is that it relates to an owner, or keeper of premises and the conceived duty to “keep an orderly house”. It doesn’t relate to a bunch of diddley players wanting to play some tunes. Any agreement for that has to be with the owner or keeper of the premises. Cases like Brearley v Morley - and several others outline this principle. Once, say, a pub landlord agrees to having music in a bar, then it is an arrangement. The landlord would then be responsible for the entertainment (whether it is entertainment for the public by the public, or some players to entertain the rest of those present).

"The music is likely to be licensable if those present at the premises are arranged as an

If you hired a band to play in a restaurant, or a pub dining room separate from the bar, then the music could be said to be incidental to the activity of eating a meal. However, if the seats were all pointed towards the musicians, those musicians might be seen as the main focus. The audience is present in either situation. That should be obvious. It’s just that the music cannot be said to be incidental.

The wording is sheight. “Audience” is irrelevant. It’s not about the presence of “an audience” but music being incidental to the main activity. If this little gem were put into the Act, it would render it “poor law”. But it was written as a result of a forum with the inclusion of a quango.
You couldn’t reasonably say that an audience isn’t present in a bar because the seats aren’t all facing towards the band.
It would mean that practically all pub music is exempt, and there is plenty of case law to show otherwise.

“Simple answer is that I don’t need to.”

Yes, you would have to state on the operating schedule how the premises will be used - that suitable arrangements were in place for health and safety of all on the premises. That would include stating that private sessions were being held in a back room, or wherever.
You could leave it in the hope that it wouldn’t come to notice. But if a licensing officer entered the premises, and was allowed access to the room without having to reveal his or her identity - voila, you have a public audience.

You do understand that licence application is made in advance, don’t you? That if there is even the potential for the public to access the room where music is being played, then it is licensable because there is nothing to say that a public audience will not be in the room at any time. That’s why the onus is on the licensee to state how the premises will be used at the time of application. It’s a premises licence, with permission or without permission to provide public entertainment. Not a public entertainment licence.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

You see, Roger, you are not thinking laterally.

Mr Puliga intended the live music to be “incidental music”.

If it comprised one musician with one instrument, in a restaurant, there is every chance that this would qualify as “incidental”. However, “incidental” is a “qualifier”. Music in a restaurant isn’t ipso facto incidental music. Mr Puliga could have omitted the mention of live music. He is not legally obliged to if he considers it to be “incidental” (though some council policies suggest that it “should” [not “must”].
So long as he kept it as intended, incidental to the main activity of dining in a restaurant, it would be fine. What if it was one musician with an overdriven Strat though? What if people complained about the noise and conditions were placed on the licence - without any provision for regulated entertainment, and stringent rules about soundproofing etc?
So, although Mr Puliga was entitled to say nothing about the intended live music, if he thought it “incidental”, it transpired that he did declare it on his operation schedule. What was the result? Mr Puliga was granted the licence variation, including the provision of regulated music (even though the music might well have come under “incidental” exemption - it was “incidental” in Mr Puliga’s opinion, anyway), though conditions were placed on the licence to ensure that the music he described was adhered to - and any other music was not to be heard outside the premises etc.
If he wanted, he could have the seats in the restaurant face the musician. He could advertise the musician as an attraction. He could even have a lute player wandering round entertaining the diners at close quarters. So long as it wasn’t someone playing an overdriven strat, or similar, and the music was inaudible outside the premises, he’s within the terms of his licence. A result. Easier on the licensing authority too, because there is ostensibly less of a chance that any complaints would be made (because conditions are already on the licence with clear terms concerning volume and number of live musicians).

This is how actually declaring the “grey area” of licensing requirements can work in the favour of all concerned. It didn’t cost Mr Puliga any extra, because he was applying for a variation of his licence in respect of extension of hours anyway.

There’s the monsters of the local authority in action.

Your head is severely up the Khyber Pass.

It’s your incoherent questions. I can only infer that you think the “incidental music” was ipso facto exempt. It’s not. It is a qualifier regarding music provided for public entertainment. It’s incidental nature has to be determined. The licensee has to decide whether in his/her opinion it is incidental. If he/she decides that it is, he/she can ignore it or put it to the authoruty to decide. The problem in going by your own decision, is, if it is later to be found as regulated entertainment, then there is a risk of “punitive” conditions being placed on the licence - or worse if ignored (as illustrated in the examples I provided). The advantage of declaring it as part of an operating schedule is it’s already acknowledged and considered. There can be no punitive measures if it’s decided by the authority beforehand. Some councils require that all activities - regulated or not- be outlined on an operating schedule (in line with objectives, but not obligatory). Some don’t. Nevertheless, there’s nothing to stop an applicant declaring all activities on an operating schedule. Signor Puliga did and it turned out to his advantage. That is the point I was making and I rather think that you got it.

Non sequitur. It is down to who is actually allowed access to the music. If it’s open to the public, then it actually matters not if there is a “public”. It relates to case law concerning a “public place” and potential “public”.

My original comment about “audience” being present among the musicians, was related to the claim that the musicians were no different than anybody else in the room (not there by arrangement to play). If that is the case, then the “public” includes that guy sitting out. If they are a group of musicians “rehearsing” (rehearsing suggests a rehearsal for a future perfomance - practice might have been better, but it makes no odds), then the mere fact that there is public access means it is potential public entertainment - and that geezer with the T shirt could come in any time - so the audience could be present any time.

Unless there is certainty that no member of the public could become an audience, then it is licensable, because the licence has to be applied for in advance.

That should be obvious. You can’t say it’s not public entertainment if you don’t know whether or not the public could walk in and become entertained -and become an audience. Even though nobody else tends to come to the session.

The only way to avoid this is to ensure that the public do not have access.

“.. every person is not active all the time…”

But if every person is “Joe Public”, then even if they are sitting and just listening, then there is a public audience.

I’ve made the point before. This is conditional on the musicians not being any different from anybody else in the place - the public, in other words.

Looked at another way, in a karaoke session, (with a live keyboard player rather than a machine) every person is not active at the same time either. One section of the public is entertaining another. The case law found that all the entertainers amounted to performers, and they were entertaining each other - which negated the “two in a bar” exemption (yes, Roger, the “two in a bar” rule is no longer applicable - it’s “none in a bar” - irrelevant -the status of those singing hasn’t altered).

And there is plenty case law to back up the point that “public access” is enough to warrant any provision of music as “public entertainment”. The key is the licensee’s prior agreement.
It’s an arranged gig - payment of the musicians is irrelevant, as is payment at the door - It does, however provide stronger evidence that the gig was intentionally provided.

Archer v Wellingrice (or Willingrice), 1802.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

If it’s a (smallish) pub, then Section 177 allows music until closing time. So your 11 pm curfew would apply if the pub closed at 11.

It’s a restaurant, so Section 177 applies only up to midnight - even if a late night refreshment facility is in place (so it’s later than your pub if your pub closes at 11) . However, the restaurant did not already have a licence in place, so your sessioneers would not have been able to go in and play unless it was incidental music.
Now permission to provide music has been granted, but the operating schedule stipulated that only one musician would be playing, so the licensing authority can hold the applicant to that number.
Your sessioneers cannot play in that restaurant, unless it’s incidental music.

No change for you, but the restaurant is now able to have one musician regardless of whether it’s incidental or not, and it can be amplified, subject to the conditions placed on the licence.

If you need anything else explaining to you, just ask. But please make your questions incoherent. The answers may seem incoherent, but that’s legal matters for you. It’s also something lawyers are able to disentangle for you, so they have more uses than the conditions you impose on them.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“If this is really the case - why would any conditions need to be imposed to duplicate what already appears on the operating schedule?”

Are you really that incompetent?

Imposing conditions that are consistent with the operating schedule, holds the applicant to the terms on the operating schedule. The operating schedule requires the applicant to state how the premises will be used, including regulated activities, and how they will be balanced with the objectives of the Act.
If the operating schedule is deemed to be kosher, then the applicant has submitted an application that conforms to the objectives of the Act. Placing conditions on the licence that are consistent with that operating schedule, effectively keeps that operating schedule kosher.

That might seem complex, but it’s quite simple and logical.

“The local authority’s other responsibilities for cultural activities would be compromised by them firstly accepting a description an operating schedule which risked deterrring or did not promote these cultural activities and secondly by imposing this as a binding licensing condition.”

What a lot of Bowlarks. You don’t understand a single bit of the guidance concerning cultural activities.

Scock horror - man applies for licence cover to provide entertainment by one musician. Council grants licence to provide entertainment by one musician.
Licence should not have been granted. The applicant should have applied for licence cover to provide entertainment by brass band (in a small restaurant) to promote local culture. Council should then have granted that cover.

“We don’t know what you mean to say - only what you actually say here”

So, when you say (quoted from above):

[That any live music will consist of one performer using an instrument not powered by electricity;]<

Perhaps you will accept that the above condition is one being imposed on small-scale non-amplified music.

S177 acts to suspend such condidtions does it not? So a session would be currently be able to take place in this venue until 11pm when the condition would once again apply.]

“We” only know what you say. And it is total bowlarks, because this assumes that the venue is open beyond 11pm (so the condition can apply) and that there is a statutory 11 pm curfew.

It is a restaurant. If that restaurant is open beyond 11pm, then the statutory curfew is midnight. It is a fixed curfew. If it is a pub (or similar) then the curfew matches the licensing hours of that pub (which is the only way that 11pm curfew could be statutory - and then the “condition would not again apply”, because the pub would be closing. You were completely off track.

“Can you please tell us if you are saying that the existing S177 would have applied in this case or not and explain your reasoning?”

No. It wouldn’t. The restaurant didn’t have provision for live music on the licence. Section 177 only applies to premises that already have provision for live music.

In order to obtain provision for live music on the licence, the applicant first has to provide an operating schedule that is consistent with the objectives of the Act.
If there are objections to the application, then the licensing authority have to hear those objections (unless all parties agree that a hearing is not necessary) and determine if those objections actually relate to the objectives of the Act. If they do, then the operating schedule should be amended to accommodate the (deemed valid) objections.
In this case, the applicant actually clarified his intentions regarding the live music provision. As regards the objections about public nuisance, amendments were made to accommodate them and the end result was an operating schedule that satisfied the objectors - and clarified the applicants wishes regarding musical entertainment.

The licence was granted. Conditions placed on the licence regarding live music were consistent with those that the applicant stated he wished to provide (his operating schedule).

If the applicant had stated that he wanted a 60 piece brass band (non-amplified) to provide entertainment, then he would also have to show how it tied in with the objectives of the Act.
If there were no objections from interested parties, then the licencing authority would be obliged to grant it - subject only to those conditions which were consistent with the operating schedule (a 100 piece brass band might be out of the reckoning). However, if there were objections, then they would have to be considered. There might be some grounds for objection to 60 brass band players in a small restaurant, in a quiet leafy terraced street (notwithstanding the Abbey across the road) giving it laldy late at night. Was it in keeping with the objectives of the Act? Well, somehow I don’t think so - but that is just a guess. It could well be that the application would have been rejected.

Anyway. Only after the cover for provision of live music has been granted does any suggestion of Section 177 come into the equation. This licence cover restricts the live music to one performer. This was what the licensee wanted. Those parameters were on the operating schedule. So long as the licensee observes that, any other conditions on the licence relating to non-amplified live music are invalid (note that there were conditions placed on amplified music that should already be in place anyway). There weren’t any (well there was arguably one, but I don’t think you’ve spotted it).
That’s how it’s supposed to work. Section 177 isn’t an exemption, and it’s not carte blanche to provide an entertainment by any number of musicians with acoustic instruments. It’s bound by the “in place” conditions of the licence.

“Because the local licensing requirement’s binding condition results in not only risks deterring, its wording actually prevents the valuable cultural activity, that is a session from taking place in this venue.”

What if Angelo Puliga doesn’t want a fecking session?

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“So it is pretty obvious that if the Licensing Authority is the Local Authority as the legislation states, then those who are employed to enforce the legislation by the Local Authority are the Licensing Authority. ”

You are showing misunderstanding yet again. Yes, the local authority are given the task of handling premises licenses.
That doesn’t mean that the whole council instantly become “the licensing authority” and have a say in whether licences are granted or not. Normally, a specific department deals with licensing, and under the Act. All licensing functions (granting or rejecting, hearings etc) are to be handled by a committee. They have the say regarding granting, refusing or conditions - within the legal requirements placed on them by the Act.

The Act clearly (for those who can actually read) states that in licence applications, the licensing authority (the licensing department of the local authority) cannot make representations. For sake of clarity, where I say “representations”, I mean “relevant representations” - which means objections neither can the licensing department apply for a review.

So, anything short of a breach (or possible breach) of licensing conditions, involves involves a process whereby licensees, interested parties or responsible authorities (which might include another local authority department, but not the licensing department) make application, and the committee’s function is to either grant or reject (if the application is invalid) or hear representations (unless agreement is made by all parties and a hearing is not necessary).

OK. that bit’s over with. All this talk of conditions, and Section 177, etc is concerned with that side.

When it comes to breach or possible breach of licensing law or conditions, then a licensing authority has enforcement teams and officers, and these might be in the same department (licensing enforcement officers) or other local authority departments - as well as the police etc.

These are “the people employed to enforce the legislation”.
It’s easy to get confused (I may well have used terms ambiguously) when “licensing authority” could mean the council, the committee, or the enforcement team etc, but that is a result of transferring the responsiblity of licensing to a local authority with several other functions.

“No, I am not mixing these up ”

The restaurant owner was granted planning permission, but he was only allowed to put six tables outside instead of the eight he originally requested permission for.
OK - now the “prohibitionist councillor”? Huddersfield operates an “alcohol control zone” in the town centre area enclosed within the A62 ring road. This prohibits anyone from drinking in the street - or even carrying open cans or bottles of alcoholic drinks. Leeds and Dewsbury have similar controls.
The restaurant owner was required to place a sign saying alcohol was not available outside - to comply with the local bye-law. A restaurannt owner applies for planning permission to put tables and chairs on the street. He gets it. Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

Let us take a case where musicians go to watch a performance.

Those musicians in the audience will be listening to those musicians who are clearly under some obligation to provide that performance.

Are those musicians sitting in the audience and under no obligation to perform - also to be described as performers in that performance? Of course not.

Those musicians in the audience and those performing on stage can still correctly be described as musicians but only those obligated to provide the performance can correctly be described as the performers.

It is the obligation to provide the performance (for the purposes etc.) which defines that the musicians are performers providing such a a performance.

Without that obligation, there can be customers making music and other customers can even be present and listening - but these are not performers who are obligated to provide any form of performance (for the purposes etc.)

The lack of this obligation is exactly why customers playing pool/darts are not currently judged to be providing a performance (for the purposes etc.). And quite correctly.

Where these customers playing pool/darts are under obligation to provide a performance (for the purposes etc.) - then this becomes licensable.

We will no doubt be told otherwise but all those activities described in Schedule 1 of the Act, as possibly being licensable, all have to be treated equally.

The following from Hamish Birchall

>The Live Music Bill will become the Live Music Act tomorrow morning when
it receives Royal Assent in the House of Lords:
http://services.parliament.uk/bills/2010-12/livemusichl.html

However, the legislation is unlikely to come into force until October.

On 27th January, when the Bill completed its Parliamentary stages, the
possibility of early implementation in time for the Queen’s Diamond
Jubilee celebrations and the Olympics was raised by Lord Colwyn and Lord
Clement-Jones, co-sponsor of the Bill with Don Foster MP.

But the statutory licensing guidance that accompanies the Licensing Act
(‘Guidance issued under s182 of the Licensing Act 2003’) must first be
substantially revised, with input from key stakeholders, including the
police and Local Government Association (LGA). This is essential if the
legislation is not to be misunderstood and misapplied by all sides, as
has so often happened in the past.

Some in the music press seem to think that the Bill marks the
culmination of a few years lobbying by musicians and the music
industry. In fact, it has taken more than 30 years of lobbying and
campaigning by musicians, backed by a coalition of the music industry,
arts organisations and performers’ unions, to arrive at this historic
moment for the regulation of live music in England and Wales.

Since at least the mid-1980s, musicians have been making representations
to central government to relax entertainment licensing because it was
hindering or actually preventing small gigs. Hopes were raised when New
Labour announced an overhaul of licensing in 1998, but dashed when it
became clear in 2002 that controls were actually to be increased, with
the scrapping of the exemption for one or two musicians in bars, and the
introduction of licensing for ‘entertainment facilities’.

When implemented, the Live Music Act will do away with the entertainment
facilities licensing requirement. The unlicensed provision of pianos,
or other instruments, for use in live performance will no longer be a
potential criminal offence.

Performances of live music between 8am and 11pm will be exempt in pubs,
bars, restaurants, schools, hospitals, and indeed all premises falling
within the definition of a ‘workplace’ for the purposes of health and
safety legislation.

For amplified music, audiences are limited to 200. There is no audience
limit for unamplified live music. In premises already licensed for
alcohol, existing conditions relating to the provision of live music
will not be enforceable for performances between 8am and 11pm. But if
there are noise problems, and complaints, a licence review could result
in enforceable conditions.

The Bill also amends the Licensing Act to allow amplified live music to
accompany performances of morris dancing or dancing of a similar nature.

Ironically, while deregulation for live music is going ahead in England
and Wales, in Scotland entertainment licensing is being increased, much
to the annoyance of those at the receiving end: http://bit.ly/A1ekNr

This is an untenable position for the Scottish government. The
rationale for entertainment licensing there is the same: to control
public safety and noise. But the legislation that regulates public
safety and noise applies across the UK. It is absurd to have within one
jurisdiction essentially the same gig legal in one part, but illegal
in another, unless licensed.

The dancers referred to in the Clarke v Searle case were doing it for “their fun”.

You had to obtain permission from the landlord for your session. This meant the landlord had committed himself to letting you use the premises for playing music. It also meant that he was allowing the premises to be used for playing music. Moreover, it was in public, and it was advertised.

“It was a fairly mean-spirited attempt to close a loophole which must have existed -”

What loophole? There was no loophole in keeping a piano. Providing a piano was found to be not enough to ascertain that a “keeper of a house” had expressly permitted public entertainment to take place in Brearley v Morley - but providing an organ for entertainment, and specifically allowing the use of a room in which the organ was kept for entertainment (though not solely for that entertainment) was considered “keeping a house for public entertainment” in Bellis v Beal. The key element was giving permission for the entertainment. The difference between Brearley v Morley and Bellis v Beal was spontaneous music and predetermined music. Even though music was frequent in Brealey’s pub (and fairly regular), it wasn’t predictable.
The provision of equipment being introduced with the 2003 Act cleared up any ambiguity (and it was a bounder who introduced that - and absolute cad), but it was the Act that made a licensee liable, not “those employed to enforce” etc.
And the keeping of a piano was not a loophole for having music on the premises. It just wasn’t enough to prove that a licensee had “kept a house for public entertainment” - until it was actually made licensable itself -.

“Is there a name for a phobia for where local government employees are terrified by and have allegic reractions to the mere mention of there being possible loopholes? ”

No. But if the law says a piano is licensable, then that’s what it is. Removing that from the Act is not likely to upset the local authority (though it might upset the odd bounder in their employ). It’s your prejudice in all this that shines through.

11 The provision of any entertainment or entertainment facilities is not to be regarded as the provision of regulated entertainment for the purposes of this Act to the extent that it consists of the provision of -

It is a licensable activity because it is a theatrical performance involving persons actually present and performing, playing a role or roles. >Entertainment facilities

(1)In this Schedule, “entertainment facilities” means facilities for enabling persons to take part in entertainment of a description falling within sub-paragraph (2) for the purpose, or for purposes which include the purpose, of being entertained.E+W
(2)The descriptions of entertainment are—
(a)making music,
(b)dancing,
(c)entertainment of a similar description to that falling within paragraph (a) or (b).
(3)This paragraph is subject to Part 3 of this Schedule (interpretation).<

I have no wish to see all games of pool and darts to be also subject to the claims made here for sessions - but it is clear that the legislation requires all the listed descriptions in Schedule 1 to be treated equally (except of course for where there are any exemptions).

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“Yes agreed - and that condition for an indoor sporting event and for all the other descriptions of possible ‘entertainments’ listed in Schedule 1 2(1) is?”

Nope. It has to qualify as “an indoor sporting event” to even get to that stage.

First it has to pass the conditions in Schedule 1, 1 (1 through 7) which are common to other activities. However, to be classed as “an indoor sporting event” even after getting through that stage, it must be (as defined in the interpretation):
[any contest, exhibition or display of any sport,
and
“sport” includes—
(a) any game in which physical skill is the predominant factor,
and
(b) any form of physical recreation which is also engaged in for
purposes of competition or display.]

So, it must be something which the licensee has provided the premises for (not the equipment - remember Mr Brearley?) and made the premises available for.

So - if Bob and Joe want a game of arrows, they may ask for the arrows from behind the bar, or bring their own (did the licensee know for sure Bob and Joe would be playing arrows that evening when he opened up in the morning?).
It must be a contest (probably would qualify) an exhibition (doubt it) or display (doubt that too) provided for the entertainment of the public, or partly for the public (an event - in sporting lingo, that means something contemplated, to be placed on a calendar or programme - look it up) where an audience or group of spectators can gather. Something premeditated - the licensee would be aware that it was happening that evening because the licensee provided it.
Not really descriptive of Bob and Joe’s game of arrows, is it?
However, if the licensee were to make sure nobody was to play the jukebox, that would help draw attention to the game wouldn’t it? Still, it doesn’t qualify as a sporting event. If the licensee were to place an ad in the local paper though, and say “darts contest Wednesday, Bob v Joe” - well it would be hard to deny as being a sporting event.

Now, does the same apply to music? Does it say “a musical event”? No. It says “a performance”, and even taking into consideration those who think that a performance means a staged event, there is the clause “entertainment of a similar description” - which doesn’t apply to an indoor sporting event.

If Roger were paid to jangle his bouzouki in the pub, Roger might regard that as a performance. If Roger just jangled his bouzouki in the pub without getting paid, Roger might not think that was a performance, but the only difference between the two is the payment. It’s still Roger jangling his bouzouki. That would be “entertainment of a similar description”. Oh yes, it’s public entertainment if the public could be entertained by it - like that councillor in the New Star enjoying the music.
Of course, if you advertise the session then it probably is a musical event. Even though the Act doesn’t stipulate that it has to be a musical event, it would be hard to argue that it was spontaneous or incidental if it was an advertised event.

Anyway, only when the “sport” can be classed as an “event” does the bit about presence of an audience etc apply.

I’m disappointed in you, Roger. I thought you would have managed that.

“It is this alone which turns anything in the following list, which in the first instance could be a description of an ‘entertainment’ that may or may not be licensable - into Regulated Entertainment or not.”

It has to fit the description in the interpretation, and not be exempted (incidental, for example) before it would qualify.

A jukebox is provided to entertain an audience (members of the public are able to listen to the music for their enjoyment) but it would only be regulated entertainment if it was set at a high volume, or a dance floor was provided.
So, no. it is not that “alone” which decides whether the entertainment is regulated or not. You also have to refer to the interpretation to decide whether the particular activity you are providing fits any of the descriptions in that list.

As this was brought up by you to somehow argue that your session should be classed the same as a game of darts, then it is relevant to point out that your session is different from a game of darts, because the Act requires that the game of darts be an event before it is licensable. Your session only has to be a performance of music or similar to be licensable.
Either have to be provided for the public etc, and the premises have to be made available for the entertainment - but it is that difference in classification that should tell you that you cannot equate your jangling bouzouki with someone throwing darts into a dartboard.
You need the rest of the Act to determine whether something is licensable.

As you are incompetent, I doubt if that will ever happen. Or at least, it will be totally irrelevant if ever you do, because by that time, your jangling bouzouki will be exempt, and all your waffling will be in vain.

If you provide a regulated entertainment even in private, then it is licensable if a charge is made with a view to profit. “Have I missed anything ?”

No. Roger is still struggling with the meaning of “sporting event”.

Why the asterisks on the “and”?

The consideration must be there, but the consideration could just be to cover the costs, and it would not be licensable - it could even accidentally make a profit - but if the intention is to make a profit then it is licensable.
Anyway, it explains why the “audience” factor is there instead of just “public” - it needn’t be a public audience.

Another thing, which is very likely a result of all those precedents ( esp Belles v Burghall) - the consideration and profit need not be for the gain of the licensee. Anyone involved in the organisation or management of the entertainment who charges for that entertainment with a view to profit (or if someone charges on their behalf) would make that entertainment licensable, but with live or recorded music, if the person playing the music chooses the music to be played and/or determines how it is played, and/or brings his/her own equipment, then that person isn’t considered to be involved in the management or organisation of the entertainment. So a musician or DJ can charge for the private entertainment and make a profit, and it is not licensable.
This would be more to do with private parties etc.

The answer must be that they could not - without changing the legislation in this way.

Soon the Live Music Bill will come into force and will mean that the route of making Regulated Entertainment via Entertainment Facilities will no longer be possible and then we will be back where we were.

Then, any attempt by those employed to enforce the legislation, to make licensable - pub customers making music for their own enjoyment - will require another change in the legislation.

↳ Posted by Roger Gall on March 20th, 2012.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“That is simple more waffle and goalpost shifting. All the descriptions of possibly licensable ‘entertainments’ are of course different from one another but all are listed together in Shedule 1. As for the purposes of licensing - they all become licensable Regulated Entertainment (or not) at the same point.”

Roger - are you going to carry on making a fool out of yourself?

Schedule 1, 1 establishes that “provision” is a premeditated action by the licensee, and that the entertainment has to be for the public (the “audience” could be private if you simply go by the descriptions). If you look at the interpretation:

[“sporting event” means any contest, exhibition or display of any sport,
and
“sport” includes—
(a) any game in which physical skill is the predominant factor,
and
(b) any form of physical recreation which is also engaged in for
purposes of competition or display.]

You will see that while darts or pool could be considered a “contest” (but would need to be more than a pub game to deem it an exhibition or display), the conditions in Schedule 1, 1 would mean it would have to be provided for the entertainment of the public for it to be classed as a sporting EVENT. That is where the guidance is taking its information from.

Live music doesn’t necessarily have to be an EVENT before it is classed as regulated entertainment - but a performance of live music or anything similar to a performance of live music would render it regulated entertainment (subject to other conditions or possible exemptions) - that “similar” aspect doesn’t apply to a sporting event.

The Act is cross referenced in several places. The list you repeatedly post is not decisive in itself.

Wise up.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

“If that were true ”

It is true. Giving express permission for the playing of music in licensed premises is providing live music.
However, giving express permission for someone to play darts, would not necessarily be provision of an “indoor sporting event”, because it has to be an “event” - not just a “performance”. If the Act were to say “a performance of sport”, there would be different connotations. Does “a performance of sport” conjure an image of someone playing sport on a stage to you? Would “performance enhancing drugs” mean something to enhance a stage performance - or something taken to “increase the performance” - render the actual carrying out of that sport action more achievable for the individual involved?

Do you see where the preconceived notion of performance takes place?
As there is no narrow interpretation of “performance” in the Act - nor any case law related to the Act, then the wider meaning has to be adopted (this is how the legal system operates).
“Performance” has the same meaning as it does in sport - and it is also consistent with the definition of performance in copyright law.

The Act says “an idoor sporting event” and “a performance of music” they have their own qualifiers and exemptions. You need to read the relevant parts of the Act in full, rather than a single paragraph to determine what is regulated entertainment or not.

>(1)The descriptions of entertainment are-
(a)a performance of a play,
(b)an exhibition of a film,
(c)an indoor sporting event,
(d)a boxing or wrestling entertainment,
(e)a performance of live music,
(f)any playing of recorded music,
(g)a performance of dance,
(h)entertainment of a similar description to that falling within paragraph (e), (f) or (g),
where the entertainment takes place in the presence of an audience and is provided for the purpose, or for purposes which include the purpose, of entertaining that audience.
(2)Any reference in sub-paragraph (1) to an audience includes a reference to spectators.
(3)This paragraph is subject to Part 3 of this Schedule (interpretation).<

It is obvious that some word has to be used in the legislation to show - for example - where the every day practice of people indulging in sport is made a licensable Regulated Entertainment. The word ‘event’ may serve this purpose in exactly the same way that the word ‘perfomance’ does for live music. No more and no less.

A few mates playing music in a pub & enjoying their own playing would not describe the activity as a performance and themselves as being performers. They may well accept such a description under different circumstances.

A few mates playing football for a local team or in an informal ’jackets-down for goal posts kickaround would not describe the activity as an event and themselves as being sportsmen. They may well accept such a description under different circumstances.

The description of entertainment and entertainers would also not be generally used to describe the above activities

Such terms as sportsman and performer are generally understood and are commonly used when describing what may also be described as entertainment and entertainers.

The attempts by those employed to enforce The Licensing Act to try and stretch the general understanding of what the public would recognise as what additional entertainment licensing permission may be required for - is the reason why the Live Music Bill was needed and passed and why this Govt’s own proposals on changes to Schedule 1 - are currently being examined.

Re: Are sessions a perfomance & are they legal in England?

As the Licensing Act 2003 currently stands, there is already provision to make activities licensable - where a pub’s customers are making music for their own enjoyment.

This by making licensable, any facility provided to enable it, like the floor on which it takes place.

This route should be preferable for those employed to enforce licensing legislation, as it could NOT also make pool & darts licensable. It does not require trying to turn anyone else who may be present - into an audience and it does not try to turn a pub customer’s into performers in a performance.

For the provision of pool tables and dart boards or even the room in which it takes place - CANNOT be a licensable Entertainment Facility - as it is only the provision of things to enable music, singing, dancing that can be licensable Regulated Entertainment as Entertanment Facilities.

So those employed to enforce the legislation do not currently need to scrape around, where a few mates playing music in a pub & enjoying their own playing, to try and turn anyone present into an audience, in order to turn this activity into Regulated Entertainment and require that additional entertainment licensing permission be obtained -do they?

When the Live Music Bill comes into force - they will no longer be able to use this route (at 11pm).
